q: Datasheets and debuggers show register values in hex, like 0xF0, rather than in decimal. Why is hex the usual choice for bit patterns?
options: A value written in hex takes less memory than the same value in decimal
One hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so 0xF0 is 1111 0000
The CPU stores and adds numbers in base 16 internally
Decimal cannot express values above 2^31, but hex can
why: 16 is 2^4, so every hex digit stands for one group of 4 bits. You can convert digit by digit: F is 1111 and 0 is 0000. Decimal digits do not line up with bit boundaries, so 240 tells you nothing at a glance.
wrong: Hex is only a way to write the number in source code or on screen. The stored bits are identical either way.
Hardware works in binary. Hex is popular because it maps cleanly onto binary, not because the CPU uses it.
Any integer can be written in either base. The limit on a value comes from the type's width, not from how it is written.

q: A status register reads 0x2A. What is that value in binary and in decimal?
why: Convert each hex digit to 4 bits: 2 is 0010 and A (10) is 1010, giving 0010 1010. In decimal that is 2 * 16 + 10 = 42.
wrong: The 2 sits in the sixteens place, not the tens place: 2 * 16 + 10 = 42.
A is 10, which is 1010 in binary. 1100 is C (12), so 0010 1100 would be 0x2C.
One hex digit is 4 bits, not 8. Two hex digits make one byte, so 0x2A fits in 8 bits.

q: A sensor's ADC returns a 12-bit unsigned reading. What range of values can the reading take?
why: n bits give 2^n different patterns. Unsigned values start at 0, so the range is 0 to 2^n - 1. For 12 bits that is 0 to 4095.
wrong: 12 bits give 2^12 = 4096 different values, but one of them is 0, so the largest is 4095.
That is the range of a signed 12-bit value. An unsigned reading has no sign bit and no negative values.
That reserves the top bit for a sign. Unsigned values use all 12 bits for magnitude.

q: On a system with 32-bit int, what does this C program print?
why: In two's complement, -x is ~x + 1. 1 is 000...001, flipping gives 111...110, and adding 1 gives all ones. So -1 is 0xffffffff, and adding 1 to all ones carries out of the top bit and leaves 0.
wrong: That is sign-magnitude: a sign bit plus the bits for 1. Two's complement does not store negatives that way.
That is ones' complement, where -1 is just 1 with every bit flipped. Two's complement adds 1 after flipping.
%x prints the unsigned bit pattern in hex. It never prints a minus sign.

q: Java's byte is a signed 8-bit two's complement integer. It can hold -128 but not +128. Why is the range lopsided?
options: One bit pattern is reserved to flag overflow, so the top positive value is lost
The sign sits in a separate ninth bit that only negatives can use
Zero uses one of the 128 non-negative patterns, so only 127 remain
-128 is really stored as unsigned 128, which only fits on that side
why: 8 bits give 256 patterns: 128 with the top bit 0 and 128 with it 1. The top-bit-1 half is -1 to -128. The other half must include zero, so positives stop at 127. In general the range is -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1.
wrong: Two's complement reserves no overflow pattern; all 256 patterns are ordinary values.
A byte has exactly 8 bits. The sign is the top bit of those 8, not an extra one.
-128 is the pattern 10000000 read as a signed value; nothing is stored as unsigned.

q: On a system with 32-bit int, what does this C program print?
why: In two's complement, flipping every bit gives -x - 1, so ~5 is -6. Adding 1 then gives -5. That is how negation works: invert all bits, then add 1.
wrong: ~x is not -x. Flipping every bit gives -x - 1, so ~5 is -6.
~ flips all 32 bits of the int, not just the 3 bits of 101. The high zeros become ones, which makes the result negative.
~x on an int is still an int. %d prints it as a signed value, so it is negative, not a large unsigned number.

q: In Java, int is a 32-bit two's complement integer whose arithmetic wraps around, and Math.abs(int) returns an int. What does this print?
why: The int range is asymmetric: -2^31 to 2^31 - 1, so +2^31 has no pattern. Negating MIN_VALUE (invert to 0x7fffffff, add 1) wraps back to 0x80000000. Math.abs documents this case.
wrong: 2147483648 does not fit in an int. The largest int is 2147483647, one less.
Math.abs does not clamp to the nearest valid value. Java int arithmetic wraps instead.
Java int overflow is silent. Only Math.absExact throws for this input.

q: You need to turn on bit 3 of the int flags and leave every other bit as it was, whether or not bit 3 is already on. Which expression does that?
why: 1 << 3 is a mask with only bit 3 set. OR forces that bit to 1 and leaves every bit where the mask is 0 unchanged, so it is safe whatever the current value is.
wrong: AND with a single-bit mask clears all the other bits. It tests or extracts bit 3, it does not set it.
XOR toggles the bit. If bit 3 is already on, this turns it off.
Adding 8 works only when bit 3 is off. If it is already on, the carry changes higher bits.

q: A driver clears one bit of a register value and then toggles another. Bit 0 is the least significant bit. What does it print?
why: 0xFF & ~0x4 clears bit 2 and gives 0xFB. Then 0xFB ^ 0x1 flips bit 0 from 1 to 0, giving 0xFA. Clearing is AND with an inverted mask, toggling is XOR with the mask.
wrong: ^ toggles, it does not set. Bit 0 was already 1, so toggling it makes it 0.
That counts bits from 1. Bit 2 is the value 4 and bit 0 is the value 1, because numbering starts at 0.
~(1u << 2) does have its high bits set, but & keeps a bit only if both sides have it. reg's high bits are 0, so they stay 0.

q: In C, == yields an int (0 or 1), 0 is false in if, and == has higher precedence than bitwise &. What does this print?
options: Compile error, as in Java: int & boolean is not allowed
It depends on the compiler: the result of x & 1 == 0 is undefined
why: == has higher precedence than &, so the test is x & (1 == 0), which is x & 0, which is 0. The else branch always runs. The fix is (x & 1) == 0. Always parenthesize bit tests.
wrong: That is what the author meant, but == binds tighter than &. The condition is x & (1 == 0), not (x & 1) == 0.
In C, 1 == 0 is the int 0, so x & 0 is a valid int expression. gcc only warns about the missing parentheses.
Precedence is fixed by the language. The expression is well defined, it just does not mean what the author meant.

q: What does this Python program print?
code:
def count(x):
    n = 0
    while x:
        x &= x - 1
        n += 1
    return n

print(count(12), count(255))
why: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and the zeros below it to 1, so x & (x - 1) clears exactly the lowest set bit. The loop runs once per set bit: 12 (1100) has 2, 255 has 8.
wrong: That is the number of binary digits. 12 is 1100, which has 4 digits but only 2 ones.
x & (x - 1) is 0 only when x has a single set bit. 12 & 11 is 8, so the loop runs again.
x &= x - 1 is not x -= 1. It removes a whole set bit per step, so it skips many values.

q: isPow2 uses the x & (x - 1) trick to test for a power of two. What does this program print?
options: true false, then an exception for 0
why: A power of two has exactly one set bit, and x & (x - 1) clears it, giving 0. But 0 has no set bits and also gives 0, so it passes wrongly. A correct check is x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0.
wrong: The trick does not handle 0. 0 - 1 is -1 (all ones), and 0 & -1 is 0, so the method returns true.
0 - 1 is just -1, a normal int. Nothing throws, and 0 & -1 is 0.
6 & 5 is 4, not 0. The test checks for exactly one set bit, and 6 (110) has two.

q: Every number in nums appears twice except one. What does this Python program print?
code:
nums = [4, 1, 2, 1, 2]
r = 0
for n in nums:
    r ^= n
print(r)
options: It depends on the order of the numbers in the list
why: a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, and order does not matter. So XOR of the whole list is (1 ^ 1) ^ (2 ^ 2) ^ 4 = 0 ^ 0 ^ 4 = 4. This finds the unpaired number in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
wrong: Only paired values cancel. 4 appears once, so it survives.
That is the XOR of the distinct values 4, 1 and 2. Duplicates cancel each other (a ^ a = 0), they do not count once.
XOR is commutative and associative, so the order does not change the result.

q: What does this Python program print?
code:
a = 3
b = 45
left = a << 4
right = b >> 3
print(left, right)
why: Each left shift by one doubles the value, so a << 4 is 3 * 2^4 = 48. A right shift by 3 divides by 2^3 and drops the remainder: 45 // 8 = 5.
wrong: Shifting by k multiplies or divides by 2^k, not by k. 3 << 4 is 3 * 16.
>> works on integers and drops the bits that fall off. It acts like floor division, so it never gives a fraction.
Shifting by k is 2^k, not 2k. 3 << 4 multiplies by 16, not by 8.

q: In Java, >> is an arithmetic right shift (fills with the sign bit) and >>> is a logical right shift (fills with zeros). -16 is 0xFFFFFFF0 as a 32-bit int. What does this print?
why: >> is an arithmetic shift: it fills with copies of the sign bit, so -16 >> 2 is -4. >>> is a logical shift: it fills with zeros, so 0xFFFFFFF0 >>> 28 leaves 0xF, which is 15.
wrong: >>> does not copy the sign bit. It shifts in zeros, so the result is a small positive number.
>> keeps the sign: it copies the top bit in, so -16 >> 2 stays negative. Only >>> fills with zeros.
A right shift does not drop the sign. >> on a negative number shifts in ones, so the result stays negative.

q: In C, x is an int holding -16. A teammate uses x >> 2 to divide by 4. What does the C standard say about x >> 2?
options: It always gives 1073741820, because C right shifts fill with zeros
It is undefined behavior, like signed overflow
It always gives -4, because C guarantees an arithmetic shift like Java's >>
why: C leaves the right shift of a negative signed value to the implementation. gcc documents it as an arithmetic shift, so you get -4, but portable code should not depend on it. Java fixes it with >> and >>>.
wrong: That holds for unsigned values. For a negative signed value the standard lets each compiler choose, and mainstream ones copy the sign bit.
Implementation-defined is weaker than undefined: each compiler must pick and document one result. Left-shifting a negative value is the UB case.
Java guarantees it, C does not. Code that needs the same result on every compiler should use x / 4 or an unsigned type.

q: On a system with 8-bit unsigned char and 32-bit unsigned int, what does this C program print?
options: Nothing reliable: both lines overflow, which is undefined behavior
why: Unsigned arithmetic is modulo 2^n. 250 + 10 = 260, and 260 mod 256 = 4. 0 - 1 wraps to 2^32 - 1 = 4294967295. This is well defined in C, unlike signed overflow.
wrong: A variable cannot hold a value outside its type. 260 does not fit in 8 bits, and an unsigned int is never negative.
C integer types do not saturate at their limits. Unsigned arithmetic wraps around instead.
Only signed overflow is undefined. Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2^n.

q: A C function guards against overflow with if (x + 1 < x) return ERROR; where x is an int. Built with gcc or clang at -O2, the guard never fires, even for INT_MAX. Why?
options: Signed overflow is UB, so the compiler can assume x + 1 > x
gcc has a bug: signed ints should wrap to INT_MIN, as they do in Java
The check is wrong only for unsigned x, which can never be negative
At -O2, ints are stored in 64-bit registers, so x + 1 never overflows
why: The compiler may assume undefined behavior never happens. Then x + 1 < x is always false and the branch can be deleted. Check before the operation instead: if (x == INT_MAX), or x > INT_MAX - y for addition.
wrong: Not a bug: C does not promise wraparound for signed ints, Java does. In C the overflow itself is the error.
It is the other way round. For unsigned x the check works, because unsigned wraparound is defined.
Register width is not the reason. The optimizer reasons from the language rules, under which the overflow cannot happen.

q: In Python, 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False. Which explanation is correct?
options: == on floats compares object identity rather than the values
It is a Python quirk: C and Java give true for the same expression
Floats keep only 7 decimal digits, so 0.3 gets cut short
0.1 and 0.2 are not exact in binary, so each is stored rounded
why: 0.1 is a repeating fraction in binary, like 1/3 in decimal, so it is stored rounded, and so is 0.2. Their sum is rounded again, giving 0.30000000000000004, a different double from the one stored for 0.3. Compare floats with a tolerance.
wrong: In Python, == compares float values; identity is the is operator. The two values really differ in the last bits.
C, Java and JavaScript use the same binary doubles and give the same false result.
Python floats are doubles with about 16 digits. The issue is binary fractions, not a digit count.

q: This Java program adds 0.1 ten times. What does it print?
why: Rounding errors make total 0.9999999999999999, so == 1.0 is false. Comparing the difference with a small tolerance, here 1e-9, is the usual fix. Pick the tolerance to fit the size of the values.
wrong: Each addition rounds, and the errors do not cancel. The total is 0.9999999999999999, not 1.0.
The error is about 1e-16, far smaller than 1e-9, so the tolerance check passes.
== has no built-in tolerance. It is the tolerance check that passes here.
